question: According to Frontex, irregular border crossings detected at the external borders of the European Union totalled just over 166 900 in the first 11 months of 20251. Eurostat reports that in 2024, some 918 925 third-country nationals were found illegally staying in the EU, 453 380 were subject to a return decision and 110 385 were actually returned2.

The Council points out, furthermore, that three out of four people who have been issued a return decision continue to stay in the EU3. This is the context in which the Commission is promoting the opening of ‘safe and legal pathways’ as an alternative way to tackle illegal immigration. 1.
On what studies is it basing the claim that expanding legal pathways reduces irregular immigration, and can it publish them?

Does it consider that offering more migration channels is an appropriate response, even though it risks sending a signal that illegal migration becomes legal, rather than effectively deterring and preventing irregular crossings?
What binding measures will it propose in 2026 to increase the effectiveness of returns (visa conditionality, financial aid, cooperation), with quantified targets and a timetable?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.3.

2026) As stated in its Asylum and Migration Management Strategy of 29 January 20261, the Commission considers that the EU approach to asylum and migration should pursue complementary objectives at the same time: prevent illegal migration and break the business of criminal smuggling networks, protect people fleeing war and persecution, and encourage talent mobility to boost the EU competitiveness.

Maintaining legal pathways, including for people in need of protection, contribute to an orderly, secure and controlled migration management system, preventing dangerous journeys and the involvement of criminal smuggling networks2. Encouraging labour and talent mobility contributes to addressing the needs of the EU labour market, and fostering innovation and competitiveness in the EU.

The Commission is continuously working to increase the effectiveness of returns and enhance cooperation with third countries on readmission. In March 2025, the Commission put forward the proposal for a return Regulation3, which aims at establishing a common EU return system, currently under negotiation.

New tools have been developed to further promote readmission cooperation by third countries, in line with European Council conclusions of 20254, such as the mechanism of Article 25a of the Visa Code, the Visa Suspension Mechanism, as well as the recently agreed revision of the Generalised Scheme of Preference Regulation5.
The Commission also proposed to extend this approach to external financing in the Global Europe Regulation proposal for the next Multiannual Financial Framework 2028-20346.

1 COM(2026) 45 final. 2 Joint Research Center, The Atlas of Migration 2025 detailing numbers of irregular and regular arrivals in 2024. 3 Directive 2008/115/EC. 4 European Council conclusions (18 December 2025, 23 October 2025, 26 June 2025). 5 Regulation (EU) 978/2012. 6 COM(2025) 571.
